transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I... well, I guess I'm here because I'm just having this terrible issue where, once a worry starts, I absolutely cannot stop it. It’s like... well, working as a media collections specialist, my whole career is about organizing information, putting things in their proper place, you know? But I just can't seem to shelve these worries in my mind. 

Once they start, they just stay there. No matter how many lists I make—and I make so many lists, I have notepads everywhere, on my nightstand, at my desk, sometimes color-coded—or how hard I try to just redirect myself to a new task, it just doesn't work. Like, I'll start worrying about my mother getting up in the middle of the night, because she's been a bit unsteady lately and I keep thinking, what if she falls when I'm not there? And then that thought just loops and loops and takes over everything. Or it'll be about work, like this big grant report we have coming up for the archives, or just this constant, nagging dread that I missed something important in the cataloging system... and I just can't turn it off. I try to tell myself to stop, I try to focus on my cataloging, but the thoughts just keep running away with me, and I really don't know how to handle it anymore.
When these worries start, do you feel driven to perform certain behaviors or mental rituals to try to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Rituals? Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't do things like... you know, flipping a light switch a certain number of times or washing my hands over and over to keep my mother from falling. It's not like that. I know some people have to count steps or repeat a specific phrase in their head to feel safe, and I actually read a very interesting article once about how that works in the brain—fascinating stuff, really, the neurobiology of it—but that’s not what’s happening with me. 

When I make my lists, which I know I just mentioned a moment ago, it’s not because I think the physical act of writing the list is going to magically prevent my mother from getting out of bed and tripping on the hallway rug. It's really just me desperately trying to dump the thoughts out of my brain onto paper because my mind is just so overwhelmingly full. So no, I don't have any routines or behaviors I feel driven to do to prevent the bad things from happening. I just... I just sit there and feel the dread. 

Like with the grant report at work, if I'm worrying about missing a deadline or miscategorizing a whole batch of archival photos from the 1920s collection we just got in—beautiful silver gelatin prints, by the way, but they require so much precise metadata—I don't do a physical action to fix the anxiety. I just sit at my desk, or lie in bed, and my stomach just ties itself in absolute knots, and I just think and think and think about all the ways it could go wrong. I don't really have a way to reduce the anxiety, which I guess is the whole reason I finally made this appointment. I just kind of drown in the thoughts until they eventually burn themselves out, which takes forever.
Do these worries happen most days and feel excessive, even when there isn’t a clear reason for them?

Oh, yes. Yes, absolutely. It's almost every single day, and I know it's excessive. I mean, I *know* it is, logically, but that doesn't stop it. And it's not even just about one or two things anymore. It's like... well, over this past year, it feels like the worry has just metastasized, if that's the right word. It used to be mainly about my mother's safety, which, you know, makes sense because she's older and she's had those unsteady moments, and I'm her primary support. But now? Now it's just spread to everything. 

I worry constantly about our finances, even though we have a budget and I track everything in a spreadsheet—I'm very meticulous about the spreadsheets, I have tabs for utilities, groceries, unexpected medical expenses, everything. But I still just sit there and fret about running out of money. And work, oh goodness, work is a whole other thing. I worry about staff decisions, whether I made the right call assigning the new intern to the oral history project versus the periodical digitization, because what if they mess up the audio files? And deadlines, of course, the deadlines are always looming. 

And it's not just the big things, either. I worry about the house—did I leave the stove on? Is the roof going to leak if it rains this weekend? The forecast said there was a thirty percent chance of rain, and I haven't checked the gutters since October. And then I start spiraling about whether I'm being a good daughter to my mother, if I'm doing enough for her, if I'm too impatient when she asks the same question twice. It’s exhausting. It feels like even the smallest, most insignificant things can just start to feel like they’re about to completely unravel my entire life. So yes, it's every day, and it just never really stops.
Have you noticed feeling down or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, like hobbies or time with friends or family?

Well, no, not really feeling down in that way. I mean, I'm exhausted, obviously, because the worrying takes up so much energy. It's like running a marathon in my head every single day. But it's not like I've lost interest in things. I still love my work with the archives, even when it stresses me out. I still get a thrill when I find a perfectly preserved piece of ephemera or when a complex metadata schema finally comes together perfectly. I mean, just last week we got a donation of personal correspondence from a local author—mostly letters from the 1960s, fascinating social history—and I was genuinely excited to start sorting through them. 

And I still enjoy my hobbies, when I can actually focus on them. I love gardening, particularly my heirloom tomatoes. I have a whole system for them, starting the seeds indoors under grow lights in February, charting their growth... though, of course, I do worry about the aphids or if the soil pH is quite right. But the interest is still there! I still want to be out there in the dirt. 

And as for friends and family, well, my mother is basically my whole world right now, and I certainly haven't lost interest in her, even if the responsibility is heavy. I still try to meet my friend Sarah for coffee on Sunday mornings, too. We go to this little place near the library, and we've been going there for years. The problem isn't that I don't *want* to go, or that I don't enjoy seeing her. The problem is that while she's talking about her daughter's ballet recital, my brain is secretly running through a checklist of whether I locked the back door or if I need to call the plumber about that slight drip under the kitchen sink. So, I'm still interested, I still care about all these things... I'm just so terribly distracted by the dread. It's not a sadness, really, just this overwhelming, loud static of worry that gets in the way of the joy.
